# AudioFile SoundObject

An **AudioFile** is a [SoundObject](soundobjects.qmd) that plays a sound file
from a SoundObject layer. Blue generates a Csound `diskin2` instrument and a
score event for it; you do not need to assign it one of your project's
Orchestra instrument IDs. This is different from an audio-layer clip, whose
timeline controls include fades and routing through the [Mixer](mixer.qmd).

## Place and select a file

1. Right-click empty space on a SoundObject layer and choose **Add
   SoundObject → AudioFile**.
2. Double-click the object to open its editor. On the **Audio File** tab,
   choose **Browse Audio File** beside **Sound File** and select a readable
   sound file. Blue displays its duration, format, sample rate, and channel
   count when it can read that metadata.
3. Move the object to its desired start position and set its **Subjective
   Duration** for the playback interval. Choosing a file changes the source
   and name; it does not automatically set the Score object's duration to
   the file's length.

The **Audio File** tab reports a missing, unreadable, or unsupported file.
For AudioFile sources, use WAV or AIFF; the file picker also offers AIFC.
The packaged macOS editor accepted stereo PCM WAV and AIFF and reported a
FLAC source as **Unsupported Audio Format**. This is separate from the
formats available for Render to Disk output. Resolve a source-file problem
before rendering. If **Copy Imported Media** is enabled
under the project's **Media** properties and the project has a directory,
Blue copies a newly selected file into its media folder; otherwise the
project keeps a path to the selected file. Keep the file available when
moving a project to another computer.

## Playback and Csound code

The **Csound** tab contains post code that receives the file channels as
`aChannel1`, `aChannel2`, and so on. Blue lists the available channel variables
for the selected file above the editor; use the post code to choose how to
route them. The default code sends the first channel to both outputs. For a
stereo file, use `outs aChannel1, aChannel2` to keep its left and right
channels distinct.

The object's start position determines when playback begins. Its Score width
sets the generated playback event's duration; it does not time-stretch the
audio. AudioFile does not apply a Note Processor chain or a SoundObject Time
Behavior to this playback event, so Score Object Properties omits those
controls for AudioFile. When a selected range starts inside the object, Blue
converts the overlap offset through the project tempo map to clip-relative
seconds before seeking into the file. Model tests cover direct placements,
direct AudioFile/FrozenObject Instances, file objects under nested PolyObjects
with unscaled, unrepeated timing, and a linked Instance whose flat PolyObject
source has a stable range-independent origin. For the latter, the Instance
and source PolyObject must use `TimeBehavior.NONE` and have no Note Processor
chains, source SoundLayers must have no processor chains, and all active direct
children must report a known origin. Sync/async tests check the translated
SoundLayer window and object-relative file overlap, seek, and finite duration.
Blue 3's stable-origin
handling is an extension to Java Blue's positional range handling for this
case. Dynamic JavaScript/Python sources, nested PolyObject/Instance leaves,
processor-bearing or transformed compositions, and GenericScore events outside
their object's subjective duration do not qualify; their existing generation
behavior remains. For example, an event at beat 2 in a GenericScore with
subjective duration 2 is pruned when the selected range starts at beat 3, so
file leaves keep the legacy seek and duration. This edge needs a separate
range-aware contract. Direct AudioFile selected-range playback has been
checked in a built macOS app with a tempo change. A packaged frozen-object
selected-range disk render matched the direct AudioFile render, realtime
playback started and finished, and the user accepted the captured output. See
[SoundObjects](soundobjects.qmd#render-from-the-middle-of-a-project) for the
range behavior. Use **Project → Generate CSD to Screen** to inspect the
generated instrument and event before rendering.

For a file you want to trim and fade directly on the timeline, use an
**audio layer** and drop a file onto it instead. See [Score](score.qmd) for
the distinction between SoundObject and audio layers.
